name: test-specific-subclass
intent: Make an otherwise untestable class testable by defining a test-only subclass that overrides the method reaching the unusable dependency (or exposes the internal state the test needs), so the boundary can be substituted and observed without putting test hooks into production code.
problem: A class that must be tested reaches its dependency through a call on itself - a self-call to a helper method, a field created inside the class, or a singleton/static lookup - so the test has no injection point: the collaborator cannot be replaced from outside, the indirect inputs cannot be controlled and the indirect outputs cannot be observed. Editing the production class to accept the dependency may be impossible (third-party or frozen code) or would introduce test logic into production.
context: Applies to legacy or third-party object-oriented code where the boundary call already sits behind an overridable (non-final, sufficiently visible) method, or can be extracted into one, and where test-only code may live next to the tests. It is a fallback for statically typed languages that need the double to stay type-compatible with a concrete class; where the code can be modified, dependency injection is the better seam.
benefits: Makes an unusable boundary controllable without touching the production class: no constructor change, no setter, no test flag, no Test Logic in Production.

Type-compatible by construction: the test double *is* the SUT type, so it can stand in wherever a variable, parameter or return value is declared with the concrete class - the case Meszaros calls out for statically typed languages.
Control and observation points (state setters, canned responses, recording overrides) live in the test tree and disappear from the production build.
Individual steps of a template-method or self-call algorithm become separately testable, and the set and order of the steps can be verified by overriding and recording them.
Cheap and local: one small subclass per test need, inheriting the real behaviour for everything that is not overridden.
Reuses the test doubles already at hand - the subclass can be a hard-coded stub, a recording spy or a configurable double - without new infrastructure.
tradeoffs: It breaks encapsulation deliberately: the test now depends on the SUT's internal method structure and inheritance details, so ordinary refactoring (rename, inline, merge of methods) silently invalidates the seam - the Fragile Tests consequence Meszaros warns about.

The seam must already exist or be carved out: a boundary buried in a long method needs Extract Method and usually a visibility change to protected, so production code is still edited, just less intrusively than by adding hooks.
The most dangerous failure is silent: if the override covers behaviour the assertion is meant to verify, the test passes while testing the double instead of the SUT.

Fragility under evolution: marking the class or the method final/sealed, privatizing a member, moving it across a module boundary or inlining the self-call kills the seam at compile time - or, in dynamically dispatched languages, leaves it silently ineffective.
Doubles built by subclassing cannot be composed freely: each additional dependency to control means another override or another subclass, and two variations cannot be combined on one instance.
The substituted-singleton flavour mutates global state from tests; without disciplined teardown it leaks into unrelated tests and hides the real production path.

participants.responsibility: Owns the untestable boundary: keeps the dependency call in a single-purpose overridable method (or an accessible field/accessor) and invokes it via self-call, so the seam can be overridden.

Test-only subclass of the SUT that overrides the boundary method with a canned, empty or recording body and/or adds accessors and state setters the test needs; packaged with the tests, never with production code.
The overridden method or added setter through which the test injects the indirect input (fixed time, canned response, forced error).
The overridden method, added getter or recording member through which the test observes indirect output, internal state or the steps that ran.
Instantiates the subclass in place of the production class (typically in a creation method), configures the control points, exercises the SUT and asserts on the observation points.
The collaborator the overridden method would reach in production - clock, network, database, mailer, singleton. In the test it is never touched: the override stands in for it.

use_cases: A legacy class reads the wall clock inside a helper method (System.currentTimeMillis, DateTime.Now, Instant.now): override the helper so date/decision logic can be tested at a fixed instant.
A reporting or notification class sends mail or calls a remote API from a self-call: override that method with a canned or empty body so the unit test runs offline and deterministically.
A class reaches a database or the file system from inside its own method: override it to return an in-memory fixture instead of building the real object chain (entity-chain snipping).
Verifying the sequence and the set of steps of a template method: override the steps in a subclass and record which of them ran, in which order.
Exposing private state for state verification, or exposing a private algorithm step so it can be tested individually (state-exposing and behaviour-exposing subclasses).
Replacing a singleton or static accessor the SUT uses through a lookup with a controlled instance that is still type-compatible with the concrete class (substituted singleton).
Putting a legacy untested class under a characterization-test baseline before refactoring, while extracting the collaborator is not yet possible.

A Java class that cannot be modified (third-party or legacy jar) but has a non-final boundary method to stub: Mockito spy() / @Spy keeps the real methods and stubs only the overridden ones - the partial mocking Mockito's Javadoc documents for legacy code and third-party interfaces (final methods stay un-stubbable).

A PHP class whose constructor opens connections or performs other side effects: createPartialMock(Class::class, ['boundaryMethod']) or getMockBuilder()->onlyMethods([...])->disableOriginalConstructor() generates a double that overrides only the named methods and skips the real constructor - PHPUnit's documented form of the pattern (final, private and static methods and enums cannot be doubled).

A .NET class with virtual boundary members: NSubstitute Substitute.ForPartsOf<T>() creates a partial substitute that - as NSubstitute's own docs state - inherits the original type via Castle DynamicProxy and runs real code except for members configured with DoNotCallBase, i.e. a generated test-specific subclass with an official 'use with caution' caveat.
avoid_when: The dependency can be injected (constructor, setter, parameter) or reached through a replaceable lookup: prefer Dependency Injection or intercepting the lookup - the subclass couples the tests to the inheritance hierarchy for no gain.

The language or test framework can replace the boundary from outside the class (monkeypatching in Python/Ruby/JavaScript, link seams in C, bytecode instrumentation such as MockK or Mockito's inline mock maker): patch that seam instead of subclassing.

The class is final/sealed, the method private/static/final, or the language has no subclassing at all (C, Go, Rust): extract an interface, trait or function pointer and inject a test double - the subclass route does not compile there.

You control the design and the code is actively changing: extract the collaborator and a real seam now (Extract Method + Self-Call + injection) instead of cementing a test-only subclass into the fixture.
The behaviour to control is not a separate call but sits in the middle of the method under test: the pattern cannot reach it - use a coarser test or refactor first.
anti_patterns: Overriding the method whose behaviour the test is asserting: the fixture replaces the logic under test, so the test can no longer fail for the right reason.
Test Logic in Production: widening the seam to public and adding test-only flags, hooks or 'if (testing)' branches to the production class instead of keeping the subclass in the test tree.
One accumulating god-subclass per SUT that carries an override for every test, with its own state and lifecycle, instead of small per-test subclasses or a Configurable Test Double.
Substituting a singleton or static boundary and forgetting to restore it, so test order becomes significant and unrelated tests silently see the double.
Keeping the subclass seam after a proper injection point has become available, out of habit - tests stay coupled to an inheritance structure that no longer needs to exist.
design_principles: Open/closed at the test seam: extend the class's behaviour for tests without modifying the class itself (production is closed for test-oriented modification).
Separation of concerns: test-specific control and observation points belong to the test fixture, never to production code.
Single responsibility and Self-Call: only a small, single-purpose method can be overridden safely; long methods must be split before they can host a seam.
Program to an interface, not an implementation - this pattern is the deliberate exception when the type is an unchangeable concrete class, and it should be documented as such.
Liskov substitution for the subclass: it must remain usable wherever the SUT type is expected, replacing only the boundary behaviour, not the contract.
Encapsulation trade-off: relax visibility to protected, never to public, and only as far as the subclass actually needs.
best_practices: Override the boundary call only; never override the behaviour the assertion is about, and keep at least one test that exercises the real dependency path.
Keep the subclass in the test source tree and instantiate it through a creation method, so production construction and the rest of the application stay untouched.
Put each boundary call in a small single-purpose method (Self-Call) before writing the subclass; if that requires Extract Method, treat the extraction as a design decision, not as test scaffolding.
Prefer the smallest seam: a canned return value for control, a recording override for observation, and a separate configurable double only when several tests share the same overrides.
Treat the seam as temporary: as soon as the class can be modified, extract the collaborator and inject it - the test subclass should not outlive the legacy constraint.
Restore substituted singletons and statics in teardown; keep tests hermetic and independent of execution order.
Document inside the test why the inheritance seam exists, so the next refactoring does not quietly break it.
sources: Meszaros, G. xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (Addison-Wesley, 2007) - Test-Specific Subclass, Test Double Patterns, Chapter 23, pp. 579-590; variations: state-exposing, behaviour-exposing and behaviour-modifying subclass, test double subclass, substituted singleton.
